answer_to_user:
Short answer: five names is NOT enough to trust as a peer average — a 5-stock mean is a thin, easily-biased sample (one outlier swings it, and all five are integrated majors, so it tells you nothing about where the majors sit within energy). Benchmark them against the broader energy-sector cohort instead. I pulled both so you can see the difference.

The whole energy sector averages a P/E of ~16.6x (computed across an 829-name energy cohort) — that is the robust benchmark. Now your five, on a currency-consistent (USD) basis:
- Shell (SHEL.LSE): P/E 10.1 · EV/EBITDA 4.4 — cheapest, and well BELOW the 16.6x sector average
- TotalEnergies (TTE.PA): P/E 10.9 · EV/EBITDA 4.9 — also clearly below sector
- Chevron (CVX.US): P/E 19.5 · EV/EBITDA 7.6 — ABOVE the sector average
- BP (BP.LSE): P/E 20.6 · EV/EBITDA 3.7 — above on P/E but cheapest on EV/EBITDA (its debt load distorts P/E; EV/EBITDA is the fairer energy multiple)
- ExxonMobil (XOM.US): P/E 21.3 · EV/EBITDA 9.4 — the most expensive

Within your five, Shell then Total look cheapest; but the key insight only shows up against the sector: your five majors AVERAGE about 16.5x P/E — essentially the SAME as the whole sector, so "cheap vs my 5 peers" would have flattered Chevron/BP/Exxon that are actually mid-to-expensive for energy. Note also BP is a case where P/E and EV/EBITDA disagree because of leverage — for energy I would lead with EV/EBITDA. Bottom line: rank the five by cheapness if you like, but judge each against the ~16.6x sector benchmark, not the 5-name average.
